name: Echinacea
summary: Alkamides and polysaccharides stimulate innate immunity. A 2014 Cochrane review of 24 trials found modest reductions in cold duration and severity; a 2007 Lancet meta-analysis found 58% lower odds of catching a cold.
how: Tea: 1-2 tsp dried root (or 2-3 tsp leaves/flowers) in 8 oz boiling water, 15 minutes, three times daily. Tincture 2.5 mL of 1:5 three times daily; extract 300-500 mg three times daily up to 10 days. Start within 24-48 hours of symptoms.
safety: Avoid in autoimmune disease (lupus, RA, MS) and with immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine and corticosteroids. Allergy risk with daisy/Asteraceae sensitivity. Not for continuous use beyond 8-10 days; pregnancy use is debated, so consult a provider.
origin: Lakota 'wind medicine', chewed for toothache and poulticed onto wounds and snakebite.

name: Goldenseal
summary: Its alkaloid berberine is broadly antimicrobial with clinical efficacy against infectious diarrhea; a 2008 Metabolism study found it lowered HbA1c and fasting glucose comparably to metformin, and it lowers LDL via PCSK9 inhibition.
how: Decoction: simmer 1/2-1 tsp chopped root in 8 oz water 10-15 minutes, three times daily. Tincture 2-4 mL of 1:10 or capsules 500-1000 mg three times daily. Cooled decoction makes a wound wash; use only sterile commercial products near eyes.
safety: Contraindicated in pregnancy (uterine stimulation, embryotoxic) and nursing (kernicterus risk). Berberine inhibits CYP2D6, CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, altering cyclosporine, warfarin and some statins, and may lower blood sugar with diabetes drugs. Limit to 3 weeks; buy cultivated (CITES-listed).
origin: Cherokee used the yellow root as a wash for skin disease and sore eyes and as a stomach bitter.

name: Black Cohosh
summary: Best studied for menopausal hot flashes and night sweats; RCTs and a 2012 Cochrane review show some benefit and German Commission E approves it. It is not a phytoestrogen but appears to act on serotonin receptors.
how: Standardized extract 20-40 mg (2.5% triterpene glycosides) twice daily, the trial form. Decoction: 1/2 tsp dried root simmered 20-30 minutes, up to three times daily. Tincture 1-2 mL of 1:10 two to three times daily; allow 4-8 weeks.
safety: Rare but serious hepatotoxicity reported: stop at once with jaundice, dark urine or abdominal pain, and avoid with hepatotoxic drugs. Contraindicated in pregnancy except at term under guidance. Caution with hormone-sensitive cancers, oral contraceptives and HRT; limit to 6 months.
origin: Cherokee women's medicine for painful menstruation and childbirth; Iroquois used it for rheumatism.

name: Slippery Elm
summary: Inner bark is roughly 50% mucilage that coats irritated mucous membranes; the FDA recognizes it as a safe and effective oral demulcent, and a 2010 pilot study found a slippery-elm formula improved IBS bowel symptoms.
how: Gruel: paste 1-2 tbsp powder with cold water, then stir into 8 oz boiling water. Tea: 1-2 tsp powder steeped 5-10 minutes, up to three times daily. Capsules 400-500 mg three to four times daily with water; powder-and-water poultice for skin.
safety: Among the safest herbs, but the mucilage can slow absorption of oral medications, so separate doses by at least 2 hours. Some sources advise against whole-bark preparations in early pregnancy. Rare allergic dermatitis; buy cultivated bark.
origin: Eastern Woodland staple: Ojibwe chewed bark strips for sore throat, Cherokee made wound poultices.

name: White Willow Bark
summary: Salicin converts to salicylic acid, the precursor of aspirin. A 2000 RCT found 240 mg salicin/day beat placebo for chronic low back pain (39% pain-free vs 6%), with modest osteoarthritis benefit; approved by German Commission E and ESCOP.
how: Decoction: 1-2 tsp dried bark simmered in 8 oz water 10-15 minutes, up to 3-4 times daily. Standardized extract supplying 120-240 mg salicin daily; tincture 3-5 mL of 1:5 three times daily. Onset is slower than aspirin.
safety: Avoid with aspirin or salicylate allergy, and never give to children or teens with viral illness (Reye's syndrome). Stop 1-2 weeks before surgery; do not combine with warfarin, heparin or NSAIDs without guidance. Avoid in pregnancy/nursing; caution in kidney disease.
origin: Used for pain and fever by nearly every nation with willows, from Cherokee to Blackfoot and Cree.

name: Saw Palmetto
summary: Fatty acids and beta-sitosterol inhibit 5-alpha reductase and DHT binding. Evidence for benign prostatic hyperplasia is mixed: European Permixon trials were positive while larger NIH trials (STEP, CAMUS) showed no benefit over placebo.
how: Standardized liposterolic extract 160 mg (85-95% fatty acids and sterols) twice daily, the trial form. Berry decoction: 1-2 tsp crushed berries simmered 10 minutes, twice daily. Tincture 1-2 mL of 1:5 twice daily; allow 4-6 weeks.
safety: Usually well tolerated (mild GI upset, headache, dizziness). Contraindicated in pregnancy and nursing due to anti-androgenic effects; caution in hormone-sensitive conditions and with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs. Urinary symptoms can signal prostate cancer, so get evaluated first.
origin: Seminole ate the berries as a staple and used berry tea for urinary and reproductive complaints.

name: Witch Hazel
summary: Tannins at 8-12% make it a strong astringent; a 2002 study found witch hazel cream matched 0.5% hydrocortisone for UV erythema, and trials show reduced hemorrhoid bleeding, itching and pain. FDA-approved OTC skin protectant.
how: Dab commercial distillate on with a cotton pad, ideally a product with added bark or leaf extract since distillation strips tannins. Decoction: 2 tbsp bark or leaves simmered in 1 cup water 15 minutes, cooled for a wash, compress, sitz bath or gargle.
safety: Topical use is very safe. Swallowing large amounts causes nausea, vomiting or liver damage from tannins, so limit internal use to small amounts of diluted tea. Alcohol-containing distillates (14-15%) dry skin and must be kept from eyes; rare dermatitis.
origin: Mohawk and other Iroquois nations introduced it to colonists as a wash for sores, bruises and hemorrhoids.

name: Yarrow
summary: The alkaloid achilleine shortens clotting time and stops bleeding, with a 2011 study showing accelerated wound closure; chamazulene and bisabolol add anti-inflammatory action and flavonoids give confirmed antispasmodic effects for cramps.
how: Crush fresh leaves straight onto bleeding wounds, the classic hemostatic use. Tea: 1-2 tsp dried aerial parts steeped 10-15 minutes, hot for fever or cool for digestion, up to 3 cups daily. Tincture 2-4 mL of 1:5 three times daily.
safety: Contraindicated in pregnancy (uterine stimulant, traditional abortifacient). Cross-reacts with ragweed and other Asteraceae allergies, and may interact unpredictably with anticoagulants since it both promotes and inhibits clotting. Never ingest the essential oil (neurotoxic thujone); large doses cause headache and vertigo.
origin: Likely the most widely used Native medicinal plant; a Navajo 'life medicine' and universal wound herb.

name: Wild Cherry Bark
summary: Prunasin releases trace hydrocyanic acid that sedates the cough reflex center much as codeine does, while scopoletin relaxes bronchial muscle. Listed in the US Pharmacopeia as a cough remedy from 1820 to 1970.
how: Cold infusion is safest: soak 1-2 tsp dried bark in 8 oz cool water several hours, then sip. Or simmer covered for 5 minutes maximum. Syrup: mix the infusion 1:1 with honey, 1-2 tsp as needed. Tincture 2-4 mL of 1:5 three times daily.
safety: Cyanide risk: use only properly dried bark, never fresh bark, leaves or cherry pits. Therapeutic doses are safe but excess is dangerous, so do not exceed recommendations. Avoid in pregnancy and nursing, reduce doses for children with guidance, and limit use to 1-2 weeks.
origin: Premier Eastern Woodland respiratory medicine; healers dried autumn-harvested bark to cut toxicity.

name: Sage
aka: Salvia apiana white sage, S. officinalis, Artemisia ludoviciana
summary: A 2011 Swiss study found sage tablets cut hot flash intensity 50% at 4 weeks and 64% at 8 weeks; S. officinalis extract improved word recall and Alzheimer's memory via acetylcholinesterase inhibition. Burning sage cut airborne bacteria 94% in one study.
how: Tea: 1-2 tsp dried leaves steeped 10 minutes, up to three times daily, gargled cooled 3-4 times daily for sore throat. Capsules 300-600 mg dried leaf three times daily; dilute essential oil for topical use only.
safety: Sage contains thujone, a neurotoxin in quantity: never take sage essential oil internally and avoid excessive amounts (culinary and tea use is fine). Contraindicated in medicinal doses in pregnancy and may reduce milk supply; thujone may lower seizure threshold. Source white sage responsibly.
origin: Sacred smudging and sweat-lodge plant across Plains, Southwest and Pacific nations; also a cold and stomach tea.

name: Cedar
summary: Cedar foliage holds about 50 mg vitamin C per 100 g, which is why Haudenosaunee 'Annedda' tea cured Cartier's scurvy-stricken crew in 1535-36. Thuja polysaccharides stimulate T-cells and phagocytosis, and the oil is antiviral and antifungal.
how: Cedar leaf tea: steep about 1 tbsp fresh or dried tips 10-15 minutes, 1-2 cups daily for colds. Steam-inhale the leaves for congestion, add a strong decoction to a bath for rheumatic aches, or dab diluted Thuja tincture on warts.
safety: Never ingest cedar essential oil: concentrated thujone is a convulsant and neurotoxin. Contraindicated in pregnancy, and prolonged use may irritate the kidneys. Identify the species correctly, since true cedars (Cedrus) differ from North American 'cedars'. Keep to 1-2 cups of tea daily, short term.
origin: One of the Four Sacred Medicines of Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee traditions, burned for purification.

name: Sweetgrass
summary: Its sweet scent comes from coumarin, which is anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and anticoagulant. A 2015 USDA study confirmed sweetgrass compounds repel mosquitoes, validating traditional insect-repellent use, and its smoke reduces airborne bacteria.
how: Tea: steep a small amount of dried sweetgrass 10 minutes for respiratory symptoms. Burn the tip of a dried braid and waft the smoke, a sacred practice to approach with respect. Place braids in closets to repel insects, or use cooled tea as a hair rinse.
safety: Coumarin is hepatotoxic in very large doses, though normal tea use is safe. Coumarin derivatives potentiate anticoagulants (warfarin itself derives from coumarin), so use caution on blood thinners. Insufficient pregnancy data, so avoid medicinal doses; source ethically, as it is overharvested.
origin: One of the Four Sacred Medicines, braided in three strands for mind, body and spirit as the hair of Mother Earth.

name: Tobacco (medicinal use)
summary: Nicotine activates nicotinic receptors and releases endorphins, giving measurable analgesia that explains the toothache remedy, and is a potent insect and parasite neurotoxin. Low-dose nicotine is anti-inflammatory via the cholinergic pathway, studied in ulcerative colitis.
how: Poultice for stings and bites: moisten a small amount of tobacco, apply 15-30 minutes, remove once pain subsides. Ceremonial offering remains a cultural, not medical, practice. Nicotine patches are the pharmaceutical route, FDA-approved for cessation.
safety: Habitual smoking or chewing causes cancer, heart disease, stroke and COPD. Nicotine is acutely toxic: never ingest tobacco, and large poultices can poison (nausea, vomiting, seizures). Extremely dangerous for children even in small amounts, absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. N. rustica holds 3-10x the nicotine of commercial tobacco.
origin: Sacred across virtually all nations, offered before harvesting, hunting and prayer, used ritually in small amounts.

name: Prickly Pear Cactus
summary: Frati's 1990 Diabetes Care study found a single dose of broiled nopal lowered blood glucose 17-46% in diabetic patients. It also lowers cholesterol, and a 2004 RCT found extract taken before drinking cut hangover severity by half.
how: De-spine the pads, then grill, saute or boil them as a vegetable or blend into juice. Capsules 500-1000 mg dried extract before meals. Eat ripe fruit fresh or as juice; split a pad and apply the mucilaginous side to burns or wounds.
safety: Lowers blood sugar sharply: diabetics on medication must monitor closely and should not combine with insulin or sulfonylureas without supervision. High fiber causes bloating and diarrhea at first and may reduce drug absorption. Glochid spines badly irritate skin; supplemental doses lack pregnancy data.
origin: Food and medicine staple of Pima, Tohono O'odham and other desert nations, with split pads laid on wounds.

name: Devil's Claw
summary: Harpagoside inhibits COX-2 and inflammatory cytokines while sparing the gut. A 2004 Cochrane review found moderate evidence for low back pain and a 2002 trial matched rofecoxib; approved by ESCOP and German Commission E.
how: Standardized extract 600-1200 mg providing 50-100 mg harpagoside daily in 2-3 doses. Decoction: 1 tsp dried tuber simmered in 2 cups water 15 minutes, in divided doses. Capsules 500-1000 mg three times daily; allow 2-3 months in chronic conditions.
safety: Avoid with active peptic ulcers (raises gastric acid) and gallstones (stimulates bile). Contraindicated in pregnancy. May potentiate anticoagulants, affect blood sugar with diabetes drugs, and case reports describe interaction with antiarrhythmic and heart medications. Buy verified H. procumbens.
origin: Apache used American devil's claw root tea for pain; the Kalahari species was Khoisan medicine for millennia.

name: Elderberry
summary: A 2004 RCT found standardized extract cut flu duration by about 4 days, and a 2019 meta-analysis of 4 RCTs confirmed reduced upper respiratory symptoms. Anthocyanins block viral hemagglutinin from binding host cells.
how: Syrup: simmer 1 cup dried berries in 3 cups water with spices until halved, strain, cool and add 1 cup raw honey; 1 tbsp daily to prevent or every 2-3 hours when ill. Elderflower tea 2-3 tsp steeped 10 minutes for fever; tincture 2-5 mL three times daily.
safety: Raw berries, bark and leaves are toxic (cyanogenic glycosides, lectin nigrin) causing severe vomiting and diarrhea, so cook the berries. Use caution or avoid in autoimmune disease, and it may antagonize immunosuppressants such as transplant drugs and methotrexate. Supplemental pregnancy data are lacking; avoid toxic look-alikes.
origin: Cherokee used berry tea for rheumatism and flower infusions for infant fevers; elderflower was a widespread diaphoretic.

name: Sassafras
summary: Traditional spring blood-purifier and fever remedy with mild diuretic, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity; safrole is documented against head lice. Root-bark safrole was banned as a food additive in 1960 after rat carcinogenicity findings.
how: File powder from the leaves contains little or no safrole and is a safe culinary spice and gumbo thickener, added at the end of cooking. Root bark tea is a legal grey area and commercial versions are often safrole-free; the decoction can be used topically for skin eruptions.
safety: The FDA considers safrole a carcinogen and large doses are hepatotoxic, so regular root-bark tea is not recommended and anyone with liver disease should avoid it. Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (embryotoxic, can cause miscarriage). Safrole inhibits CYP enzymes, altering drug metabolism, and is an MDMA precursor.
origin: Cherokee spring tonic and fever remedy; Choctaw ground the leaves into file powder, still used in Creole cooking.

name: Wild Ginger
summary: Carminative and antiemetic root with demonstrated antimicrobial activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria plus antifungal effects; some sesquiterpenes show preliminary antiarrhythmic activity matching Iroquois use for heart conditions.
how: Tea: steep 1 tsp dried chopped root in 8 oz hot water 15 minutes for digestive upset or colds. Use the dried root as a culinary ginger substitute, or poultice crushed fresh root on minor wounds.
safety: Contains aristolochic acid, a known nephrotoxin and carcinogen linked to kidney damage and urothelial cancer. Occasional short-term use of small amounts appears low risk, but regular or chronic use is not recommended. Contraindicated in pregnancy; avoid entirely with kidney disease.
origin: Great Lakes nations used it as a stomach soother and to make bitter medicines palatable; also an ear remedy.

name: Bee Balm
aka: wild bergamot, Monarda fistulosa, Oswego tea
summary: Naturally rich in thymol and carvacrol, the proven antiseptics in Listerine. A 2012 study demonstrated potent anti-MRSA activity, with confirmed action against E. coli, Salmonella, Pseudomonas and Candida plus carminative effects.
how: Tea: 1-2 tsp dried leaves and flowers steeped 10-15 minutes, up to 3 cups daily, or gargled for sore throat. Apply crushed fresh leaves to minor skin infections and bites, steam-inhale for sinus congestion, or cook with it like oregano.
safety: One of the safest plants here. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy, since thymol in quantity stimulates the uterus (culinary amounts are fine). Possible cross-reactivity with mint/Lamiaceae allergies; never ingest undiluted essential oil, as concentrated thymol irritates mucous membranes.
origin: Ojibwe inhaled leaf decoction for colds; Oneida taught colonists Oswego tea during the Boston Tea Party era.

name: Chaparral
summary: Its NDGA is one of the most potent natural antioxidants and a lipoxygenase inhibitor with broad antimicrobial activity. Anticancer findings are laboratory-only, so any role would be complementary support at most, with no human efficacy proven.
how: Topical use is safest: simmer leaves and stems and use the wash for skin conditions, wounds or fungal infections. Steam inhalation for respiratory congestion is traditional and relatively safe. Internal capsules and tinctures are sold but carry real hepatotoxicity risk.
safety: Serious liver damage, including hepatitis, cirrhosis and failure requiring transplant, has followed internal use; the FDA warned consumers in 1992. NDGA also causes kidney lesions at high doses and inhibits cytochrome P450 enzymes. Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and liver disease; internal use is not recommended.
origin: The most important medicine of Sonoran and Mojave desert peoples, drunk for colds and used in steam baths.

name: American Ginseng
summary: A 2005 CMAJ RCT found a standardized extract reduced upper respiratory infections in older adults, and 3 g cut postprandial glucose 20% in type 2 diabetes. As complementary support, 2000 mg daily reduced cancer-related fatigue in a Mayo Clinic trial.
how: Tea: 1-2 tsp sliced dried root simmered 15-20 minutes, 1-2 cups daily. Standardized extract 200-400 mg (4-7% ginsenosides) once or twice daily, or capsules 500-2000 mg dried root daily. Best cycled 2-3 weeks on, 1 week off.
safety: Common effects are insomnia, headache and digestive upset. May reduce warfarin effectiveness (case reports of lowered INR) and add to diabetes medications. Weakly estrogenic, so use caution in hormone-sensitive conditions, and avoid with MAO inhibitors. Pregnancy data are insufficient; buy cultivated root only.
origin: Cherokee 'mountain climber', one of their most important plants; Ojibwe added it to formulas to boost potency.

name: Boneset
summary: Sesquiterpene lactones and polysaccharides stimulate phagocytosis and macrophage activity, with animal-confirmed fever reduction and in vitro antiviral activity against influenza. German Commission E approves it for colds and fever.
how: Hot tea as a diaphoretic: 1-2 tsp dried aerial parts steeped 10-15 minutes, up to 3 cups daily (very bitter). The same brew cooled completely was the traditional tonic and laxative. Tincture 2-4 mL of 1:5 three times daily.
safety: Contains hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids, so never use long term: limit to acute illness, 1-2 weeks maximum. Contraindicated in pregnancy, nursing and liver disease. Large doses cause vomiting, and Asteraceae allergy sufferers may react.
origin: Named for treating the deep aches of 'break-bone fever'; a leading Eastern fever medicine adopted by settlers.

name: Evening Primrose
summary: Seed oil supplies 7-10% gamma-linolenic acid, a precursor to anti-inflammatory PGE1. A 2013 meta-analysis found improved eczema symptoms (a Cochrane review found evidence insufficient), and an RCT showed 480 mg GLA/day improved diabetic neuropathy.
how: Capsules 500-1000 mg EPO (40-80 mg GLA each), 2-6 capsules daily, with higher doses for eczema and rheumatoid arthritis. Apply the oil directly to dry or eczematous skin. Allow 8-12 weeks of consistent use.
safety: Generally very safe; mild GI upset and headache are most common. It may lower seizure threshold, so use caution in epilepsy or with phenothiazine drugs. GLA is mildly antiplatelet: use caution with anticoagulants and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Pregnancy data are insufficient.
origin: Cherokee applied the whole plant as a poultice for hemorrhoids and bruises; roots and seeds were eaten as food.

name: Bloodroot
summary: Its alkaloid sanguinarine is broadly antimicrobial and once featured in dental products that cut plaque and gingivitis, but chronic oral exposure was linked to leukoplakia and products were withdrawn. Laboratory anticancer findings have produced no approved application.
how: Not a plant for self-medication. It is no longer in mainstream dental products, though a few herbal toothpastes use very low concentrations, and some herbalists use very dilute topical preparations for warts under expert guidance only.
safety: Bloodroot 'black salve' is a caustic escharotic that destroys healthy tissue non-selectively, causing disfiguring wounds, scarring and necrosis; the FDA calls it a fake cancer cure and has sued vendors. Never use it on cancer or skin lesions. Internally sanguinarine causes vomiting, CNS depression and cardiac toxicity, with deaths reported; contraindicated in pregnancy.
origin: Cherokee applied the red root juice to skin growths; Ojibwe took it on maple sugar for sore throat.

name: Blue Cohosh
summary: Caulosaponin stimulates uterine contractions in animal models, and N-methylcytisine both stimulates the uterus and relaxes smooth muscle depending on dose, explaining its dual traditional use. Serious adverse events have curtailed modern research.
how: Not recommended for self-use. If used at all, only under direct supervision of an experienced midwife or clinical herbalist. It was historically a root decoction, but dosing is critical and the therapeutic window is narrow.
safety: Case reports document severe neonatal harm when mothers used it near term, including myocardial infarction, heart failure, seizures and stroke. N-methylcytisine is nicotine-related and can cause cardiovascular toxicity including coronary vasospasm. Contraindicated for self-use in pregnancy despite its traditional labor role.
origin: Cherokee and Iroquois women's medicine to facilitate childbirth and regulate menstruation.

name: Bearberry
summary: Arbutin is converted by gut bacteria to hydroquinone, excreted renally to create antiseptic action right in the urinary tract. German Commission E approves uva ursi for lower urinary tract inflammation, with activity against E. coli, Proteus and Staphylococcus.
how: Cold infusion preferred: soak 2-3 tsp dried leaves in 8 oz cold water 12-24 hours, then drink 3-4 cups daily; this limits stomach-upsetting tannins. Capsules 400-800 mg (20% arbutin) three times daily. Efficacy needs alkaline urine, so pair with baking soda.
safety: Long-term or high-dose use accumulates hydroquinone, causing liver damage, retinal toxicity and GI irritation: limit to 1-2 weeks and 5 courses a year. Contraindicated in pregnancy, nursing, children under 12 and kidney disease. Seek care if UTI symptoms last beyond 48 hours or fever or flank pain appear.
origin: Central to kinnikinnick smoking mixtures; Blackfoot, Cheyenne and Cree used leaf tea for urinary infections.

name: Black Raspberry
summary: Holds up to 3x the anthocyanins of red raspberries. As complementary support, Ohio State research found black raspberry lozenges reduced precancerous oral lesions. Root-bark tannins explain the validated antidiarrheal use.
how: Eat fresh or frozen berries regularly, or use freeze-dried powder. Root bark tea for diarrhea: 1 tsp simmered 15 minutes, three times daily. Raspberry leaf tea in pregnancy: 1-2 tsp steeped 10 minutes, from the second trimester at 1 cup daily, rising to 2-3 in the third.
safety: Berries and leaf tea are extremely safe. Avoid raspberry leaf tea in the first trimester due to uterine-stimulating effects. Overused root bark can constipate from high tannins, and very high berry intake may mildly thin the blood.
origin: Cherokee used root bark tea for diarrhea and dysentery; raspberry leaf was widespread for uterine toning.

name: Chokecherry
summary: Shares wild cherry's pharmacology: bark prunasin suppresses the cough reflex, while high tannin content gives effective astringent antidiarrheal action. Berries are rich in anthocyanins, vitamin C, iron and manganese.
how: Always cook chokecherries before eating, since heat destroys cyanogenic compounds; use in jams, syrups and sauces. Bark tea follows the wild cherry method, a short decoction of dried bark. Traditional pemmican pounds dried berries with dried meat and rendered fat.
safety: Same cyanide warnings as wild cherry bark: leaves, bark and especially pits contain cyanogenic glycosides, so cook the berries, dry the bark and never eat raw pits. Wilted leaves and fresh bark are especially dangerous; avoid bark preparations in pregnancy.
origin: A cornerstone Plains food and medicine, central to pemmican and used as bark tea for cough and sore throat.

name: Juniper Berry
summary: Terpinen-4-ol raises glomerular filtration for a diuretic effect without the electrolyte loss of thiazides, supporting traditional kidney and bladder use; the oil is antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory. German Commission E approves it for dyspeptic complaints.
how: Tea: lightly crush 1 tsp dried berries, steep 15 minutes, up to 3 cups daily. Dilute the essential oil to 2-3% for arthritic joint massage, or use berries as a spice with game meats and stews.
safety: Contraindicated in kidney disease, since the volatile oil irritates the kidneys, and high doses cause hematuria and kidney damage. Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy: it is a uterine stimulant that can cause miscarriage. Limit to 4-6 weeks, monitor blood sugar on diabetes medications, and confirm the species.
origin: Sacred to the Navajo and burned in sweat lodges; Lakota and Cree drank the tea for kidney and bladder problems.

name: Passionflower
summary: Flavonoids and harmine bind GABA-A receptors like benzodiazepines. A 2001 RCT found it as effective as oxazepam for generalized anxiety with less performance impairment, and a 2011 RCT showed improved sleep; approved by German Commission E, ESCOP and EMA.
how: Tea: 1-2 tsp dried aerial parts steeped 10-15 minutes, 1 cup 30-60 minutes before bed or up to 3 cups daily for anxiety. Tincture 1-4 mL of 1:5 three times daily; capsules 400-500 mg standardized extract once or twice daily.
safety: Generally very safe, with possible drowsiness and dizziness. Enhances benzodiazepines, barbiturates and alcohol, so use caution with any CNS depressant, and harmine is a weak MAOI, giving theoretical interaction with MAOI drugs. Contraindicated in pregnancy; stop 2 weeks before surgery and avoid driving.
origin: Cherokee used root poultices for boils, cuts and earaches; Houma used the roots as a blood tonic.

name: Osha Root
summary: Traditional remedy for respiratory infections, sore throat, cough and altitude sickness. Z-ligustilide and related phthalides show anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and smooth-muscle-relaxing activity, though clinical trials are limited.
how: Used as root tea, tincture or chewed root for coughs, sore throat and chest congestion, following product dosing from reputable suppliers.
safety: Do not wildcraft: osha is overharvested and slow-growing, and its look-alikes include poison hemlock and water hemlock, making foraging lethal for the inexperienced. Buy only correctly identified material from trusted sources.
origin: Navajo, Apache, Zuni, Taos Pueblo and Ute 'bear medicine' for the lungs.

name: Cascara Sagrada
summary: Powerful stimulant laxative whose anthraquinone glycosides drive colonic motility. It was an official USP drug for decades and an FDA-approved OTC laxative until 2002, when it was reclassified for insufficient modern safety data rather than proven harm.
how: Bark preparations are taken short term for constipation at the lowest effective labeled dose, and only occasionally.
safety: Habit-forming: long-term use causes 'lazy bowel' dependence and electrolyte disturbances, which can compound diuretics and digoxin. Reserve for short-term use and address chronic constipation with diet, fluid and medical evaluation.
origin: Used as a laxative by Salish, Chinook and other Pacific Northwest Coast peoples.

name: Fireweed
summary: Used for prostate health, wound healing and diarrhea. It contains oenothein B, a polyphenol that inhibits 5-alpha-reductase and aromatase, and European clinical evidence supports its use for benign prostatic hyperplasia.
how: Traditionally taken as a leaf tea; standardized European products are used for BPH symptoms per label dosing.
safety: Because it alters androgen metabolism, use caution with hormone-sensitive conditions and with prostate or hormonal medications. Prostate symptoms need medical evaluation to rule out cancer before self-treating.
origin: Used by Ojibwe, Cree and many Northern nations.

name: Black Walnut
summary: Traditional antifungal for ringworm and athlete's foot, plus antiparasitic and astringent uses. Its primary compound juglone has documented antifungal, antibacterial and anthelmintic activity in multiple studies.
how: Applied topically as hull preparations or tincture for fungal skin infections; internal use should be limited and short term.
safety: Juglone is cytotoxic at high doses, so use topically rather than internally in large amounts. Tree-nut allergy is a contraindication, and high tannin content may reduce absorption of oral medications taken at the same time.
origin: Used by Cherokee, Comanche, Rappahannock and Iroquois.

name: Spicebush
summary: Used for colds, fever, cough and rheumatism and as a pleasant beverage tea. It contains terpenoids and flavonoids with anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity, though it is less studied than most remedies here.
how: Twigs, leaves or berries are steeped as an aromatic tea and drunk for colds and fever.
safety: No specific interactions are documented, but safety data are thin: avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy and nursing, and consult a provider if you take prescription medications.
origin: Used by Cherokee, Rappahannock, Iroquois and Ojibwe.
